extracted.intended_audience: members of the Chemical Society; academic and industrial chemists; educational policymakers in the UK
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and desiderata for organising, funding, staffing, and evaluating chemical research across universities, technical schools, and factories, and for distributing research scholarships and grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public appreciation beyond utilitarian outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific research should not be judged solely by proximate practical results; 'the public cannot, as matters now exist in this country, go behind such proximate results.' Science is often 'measured solely by the utilitarian standard.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for raising public opinion to value research as a cultural good (on parity with literature and art) whether or not it leads to immediate industrial applications. Anti-pattern: limiting appreciation to immediately saleable outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of pure and applied science (no antagonism)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be no antagonism between pure and applied science; 'the course of industrial development in the future is bound to become more and more interwoven with the development of pure science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages re-adjustment of public and institutional positions so pure and applied work are allies. Evidence: coal‑tar industry progressed as pure science substituted for empiricism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities judged by quantity and quality of research output
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities should be productive centres of research; judged by both quality and quantity of contributions — many British universities are 'distinct failures as centres of chemical research' compared with Continental counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should compare publication output and substantive contributions with international standards. Anti-pattern: accepting low output because of tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modernise educational methods (avoid defective methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defective educational methods and ancient traditions hinder research; the modern technical education movement has not yet fulfilled expectations for advancing chemical science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should revise pedagogy and curricula to promote original work rather than rote or purely examinational success. Example problem: 'the trail of the examining board' undermines research spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/Polytechnic institutions must support original research
rubrics_metrics.description: New technical institutions (polytechnics) should not be merely cramming establishments; a 'school of chemistry which is not also a centre of research is bound to degenerate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must provide time, facilities and a research culture so teachers and students can pursue original investigations. Anti-pattern: running institutions primarily to meet grant-earning or board exam requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate endowment and maintenance funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient endowment is essential; inadequate provision for maintenance forces institutions to lower standards and run as 'purely business concerns.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding should prioritise sustaining research activity (not only buildings/equipment) to avoid trading off research quality for short-term financial metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint strong scientific leadership and staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the principle 'First find a curator and let him build his museum around him' — success depends on individual teachers/leaders who can create schools of chemistry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit leaders who combine teaching excellence and original-investigator zeal. Anti-pattern: appointing administrators or office staff over scientific leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance should value scientific staff over administrative/business concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevalence of the 'business' spirit among committees gives exaggerated importance to office staff while undervaluing scientific staff whose work 'is generally beyond' the comprehension of average committeemen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governing bodies should recognise scarcity of really good teachers and investigators and resist metrics that privilege easily‑measured administrative outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect teachers' time for research (limit administrative/teaching overload)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers overloaded with teaching, administrative duties and routine 'drudgery of coaching' are prevented from doing original work and become 'chemical schoolmasters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should structure duties so promising researchers have time and energy for original investigations; avoid annual rote teaching cycles that strangle research spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide adequate remuneration to attract and retain talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale of remuneration for chemical teachers in newer institutions is often inadequate (sometimes below artisan wages) and deters recruiting/retaining the best teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive pay is necessary, though not sole determinant; combined with research facilities it encourages talented young chemists to accept posts even at early career stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor curricula to professional requirements (avoid one‑mould education)
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should not be rammed 'into one mould' irrespective of differing requirements (e.g., engineers vs chemists); inappropriate generalisation harms chemistry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design course content and training pathways specific to the needs of chemical science rather than a uniform technical syllabus that fritters teaching time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factories as genuine centres of research (well‑staffed labs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical factories should host recognised, well‑staffed research laboratories; current practice often degrades promising chemists into routine testers ('mere machines').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry should employ 'real scientific chemists' and develop laboratories comparable to those in leading German colour factories. Anti-pattern: factories that only perform routine testing requiring little chemical education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster cooperation between industry and educational establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperation between manufacturers and teachers links education and industry productively; its absence breeds distrust and cripples both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage formal relationships and collaborations so educational training aligns with industrial needs and industry benefits from research talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use targeted research scholarships selected by teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: Award research scholarships to men of proved ability, selected by teachers who know students' real (not purely examinational) capabilities, to enable original work post‑training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarships capture the 'right men' through informed selection rather than mass exam-based allocation; this is a highly valuable counteracting agency against talent wastage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable, efficient distribution of research funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Research grant committees must equitably prune applications because demand exceeds funds; 'the main difficulty of administration is the equitable pruning of the various applications.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute funds across branches while seeking the best returns; keep transparent criteria and balance breadth vs depth of support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund allocations should include personal grants to hire skilled assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond materials and apparatus, allotting personal grants to enable grantees 'to secure skilled assistance' (human material) would notably increase quantity and quality of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift some grant practice from only buying apparatus to subsidising labour/support personnel; requires larger income/capitalisation but yields higher returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure fund impact by publications and publication rate per grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess research-fund effectiveness by outputs: number of grantees, papers published, failures to publish, and cost per paper (example: grants averaged ~8–9 pounds per paper in cited period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete metrics (papers per grant, papers per pound) to demonstrate high returns on modest research funds and justify further capitalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalise and expand research funds to scale impact
rubrics_metrics.description: To make substantial personal grants and broader support, the research fund must be capitalised to deliver incomes of thousands rather than hundreds per annum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long‑term fundraising/capital campaigns are recommended to increase the income available for more effective grant types (personal support, skilled assistance).
